questions.qtext: Which of the following statements is/are true ?

options.text: Lexical analysis is recursive in order to handle nested parentheses.
Scanners don't know anything about the grammar of a language.
A regular expression is a type of pattern used to classify lexemes.
You can change state in a DFA without reading any input character.

questions.solution:
Answer: B, C

Source solution 1 (score: 4)

A is false – Lexical analysers cannot handle nested structures. Why? Because lexers use regular expressions, and regular languages cannot count or match nested parentheses. Nested parentheses require context-free grammar, which is handled by the parser, not the lexer.

B is true – Scanners only recognise tokens and do not know grammar rules.

C is true – Regular expressions are exactly the patterns used to classify lexemes in lexical analysis.

D is false – DFA has no ε-moves. It cannot change state without consuming an input symbol.

Correct statements: B and C

Source solution 2 (score: 3)
Lex cannot be used to recognize nested structures such as parentheses.
Source solution 3 (score: 2)

Correct Statements: B and C

Here is the detailed analysis of each statement:

  • A is False: Lexical analysis is implemented using Finite Automata (based on Regular Grammars). Finite Automata do not have auxiliary memory (like a stack) to keep track of counting, so they cannot handle arbitrarily nested parentheses. Nested structures are handled by the next phase, the Syntax Analyzer (Parser), which uses a Pushdown Automaton.

  • B is True: Scanners (Lexical Analyzers) simply group streams of characters into tokens based on Regular Expressions. They do not know anything about the structural syntax or the context-free grammar of the programming language.

  • C is True: A regular expression is formally used to define the pattern for a token. When a sequence of characters in the source code matches this defined pattern, that specific sequence is called a lexeme.

  • D is False: By definition, a DFA (Deterministic Finite Automaton) must consume exactly one input character for every state transition. Changing states without reading an input character is called an epsilon-transition (or null transition), which is only allowed in an NFA, not a DFA.
